Web development for small businesses is often evaluated by familiar criteria: speed, CMS, design, forms, ease of editing, integrations. All of that matters. But it seems to me that one architectural criterion is discussed far too rarely: whether the site and the associated digital layer can be properly taken over and transferred without losing manageability. If not, then what we have is not just a technical solution, but a mechanism of dependency.

- From an engineering standpoint, it is useful to distinguish between a “working website” and a “transferable digital asset.” The former may be quite convenient to operate. The latter requires additional properties: a domain under the Owner’s control, a clear access model, exportability of content and structure, no critical dependency on a single contractor, and a documented current state. Without this, the system performs its functions but remains poorly transferable.
- It is especially interesting how this affects information architecture. When a project is built from the outset as an asset, URLs, templates, content entities, the media library, backups, and even editorial processes are designed differently. Development becomes less decorative and more systemic: the site is viewed not as a storefront, but as part of the business’s manageable infrastructure.
- In practice, the problem rarely appears as a purely technical one. It surfaces when changing agencies, transferring the business, dealing with access conflicts, or trying to migrate carefully without losing leads and structure. And then it turns out that the solution that seemed “simple” was simple only on the way in, not on the way out.

Do you consider designing a proper exit and transfer scenario to be a mandatory part of good web development for small businesses?
